answer_text:
Let \(d=\deg P\). We will show that the only possible degree is \(1\).

---

### 1. The sequence \((a_i)\) tends to infinity

Since the \(a_i\) are distinct natural numbers, for every fixed \(M\) only finitely many of them are \(\le M\). Hence

\[
a_i\to\infty \qquad \text{as } i\to\infty.
\]

So in particular \(a_{i+1}\to\infty\).

---

### 2. Degree \(0\) is impossible

If \(P\) were constant, then \(P(a_1)=0\) forces \(P(x)\equiv 0\). But then

\[
P(a_{i+1})=0=a_i
\]

for every \(i\), so all \(a_i\) are equal, contradicting distinctness. Thus \(d\ge 1\).

---

### 3. No degree \(d\ge 2\) is possible

Suppose \(d\ge 2\). Write

\[
P(x)=c x^d+\text{lower-degree terms},
\qquad c\ne 0.
\]

Because \(P(a_{i+1})=a_i>0\) for all sufficiently large \(i\), the leading coefficient must be positive; otherwise \(P(x)\) would be negative for all sufficiently large \(x\). Thus \(c>0\).

Now divide the identity \(P(a_{i+1})=a_i\) by \(a_{i+1}\):

\[
\frac{a_i}{a_{i+1}}
=
\frac{P(a_{i+1})}{a_{i+1}}
=
c a_{i+1}^{d-1}+\cdots+c_1.
\]

Since \(d\ge 2\) and \(a_{i+1}\to\infty\), the right-hand side tends to \(+\infty\). Therefore,

\[
\frac{a_i}{a_{i+1}}\to+\infty.
\]

In particular, for all sufficiently large \(i\),

\[
\frac{a_i}{a_{i+1}}>1,
\]

so

\[
a_i>a_{i+1}.
\]

Thus the tail of the sequence is a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, which cannot be infinite. This contradiction shows that \(d\not\ge 2\).

Hence the only possible degree is \(1\).

---

### 4. Degree \(1\) is attainable

Take

\[
P(x)=x-1
\]

and

\[
a_i=i \qquad (i=1,2,3,\dots).
\]

Then

\[
P(a_1)=P(1)=0,
\]

and for every \(i\ge 1\),

\[
P(a_{i+1})=P(i+1)=i=a_i.
\]

The numbers \(a_i=i\) are distinct natural numbers, so degree \(1\) is indeed possible.

Therefore, the possible degree of \(P\) is exactly

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
